title: Balcony and plug-in solar PV: what is now legal in the UK
subtitle: Understanding the 2024 rule change that allows small plug-in solar panels without an electrician
excerpt: From 2024, the UK allows households to plug a small solar panel directly into a standard 13-amp socket without a registered electrician, provided the system meets specific requirements. These balcony or plug-in solar systems are widely used in Germany and France and are now a legal option for UK flats and houses without a south-facing roof.
sourceNotes: UK Government consultation response on microgeneration permitted development (2024); BS 7671 Amendment 4 on plug-in microgeneration; Ofgem Smart Export Guarantee guidance on sub-800W systems.

glossaryTerms.definition: Solar photovoltaic panels that convert sunlight into electricity directly, as distinct from solar thermal collectors that heat water.
A small inverter attached directly to a single solar panel, converting DC output to AC mains voltage. Used in balcony solar systems to allow direct connection to a household circuit.

content.text: A plug-in solar system is one or two

that converts the panel output to 230 V AC and feeds it into a standard household socket. These systems are very common in Germany (called Balkonkraftwerk) and France. A 2024 UK legislative change and updated wiring standards have made them legal here for systems up to 800 W connected to a standard 13-amp socket.
Systems up to 800 W connected to a standard 13-amp socket, no notifiable electrical work required.
The system must use a Schuko or UK-style plug connection. Anti-back-feed protection must be built into the inverter.
The socket used must be in good condition; do not plug into an extension lead or a socket that shows signs of loose pins.
Notify your electricity network operator. Most urban properties are in a G98 area. The registration is a simple online form, not an approval process.
Realistic generation from a balcony system

A single 400 W panel on a south-facing balcony rail at 30 to 40° tilt generates approximately 300 to 400 kWh per year in southern England. Most of that generation displaces electricity you would otherwise import. The savings are higher if the panel is running during peak-tariff hours on a time-of-use tariff.
Limitations and what to check first
Leasehold flats: check the lease before attaching anything to a balcony railing. Balcony railings are usually in the common parts. Freeholder consent is normally required.
Conservation areas: a panel on a balcony facing a highway may need planning permission. The same rules apply to balcony panels as to roof panels.

Smart meter: if you have a non-smart meter, the meter cannot measure export and you will not be paid for any surplus electricity sent back to the grid. With a SMETS2 meter and SEG registration, even a sub-800W system can earn export payments.

Panel mounted at 30 to 40° tilt on a purpose-built balcony bracket with stainless fixings. Inverter cable managed with cable clips rather than hanging loose. Plug connected to a dedicated socket, not a shared extension. Monitoring app showing generation matches expected output for the angle and season.

rows.symptom: Micro-inverter does not appear online despite being connected
rows.cause: Inverter requires 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi to report data; some home networks only broadcast 5 GHz
rows.fix: Enable the 2.4 GHz band on your router (most modern routers broadcast both simultaneously but may need enabling in settings).

rows.symptom: Household energy monitor shows import not falling during daylight generation
rows.cause: Loads in the house exceed generation; the panel output is consumed silently at source
rows.fix: This is normal and correct operation. Generation reduces import; it does not drive import to zero unless the panel output exceeds all current loads.
